claim: NixOS expresses systemd user services via systemd.user.services.<name>, managed by the user's own systemd instance so a user can start/stop/restart services without sudo
stance_target: user-scoped systemd services are a viable mechanism for running an agent without granting sudo
scope_conditions: NixOS with systemd; user services only
quoted_support: In NixOS, a user service can be expressed with systemd.user.services.<name> ... This may be useful if you want a user to be able to start, stop, and restart their own instance of a service without needing to make the user a sudoer.
time_period: wiki page oldid 27204 (current as of Sep 2026)

claim: By default user services stop at logout and restart only on next login (wantedBy = default.target); keeping a user service running after logout requires users.users.<username>.linger = true, plus wantedBy = [ "multi-user.target" ] for boot-time start
stance_target: fleet-wide headless deployment of a user-scoped agent on NixOS requires explicit lingering configuration, not the default user-service wiring
scope_conditions: NixOS user services; headless or no-login hosts
quoted_support: If you need a user service to stay running after a user logs out, you need to enable "lingering" by setting users.users.<username>.linger = true; You'll also likely want to change to wantedBy = [ "multi-user.target" ]; so the service starts at boot time.

claim: Enabling a systemd.user.services unit in NixOS installs it for EVERY user for which systemd spawns a user manager; restricting it to specific users requires unitConfig.ConditionUser (e.g. "UserA|UserB" or "!root")
stance_target: a NixOS user-service-based agent install must gate execution per-user via ConditionUser, since unit installation is system-wide by default
quoted_support: By default, enabling a user service enables it for every user for which systemd spawns a service manager. If you wish for the service to be run only for specific users (say, UserA and UserB), use ConditionUser (man 5 systemd.unit).

claim: Interaction with user services uses systemctl --user (status) and journalctl --user-unit <name> for logs, and the NixOS wiki itself defers to the Arch wiki systemd/User page for fuller background
stance_target: operational debugging of a fleet agent running as a user service
quoted_support: To interact with user-specific systemd services, use the --user flag with the systemctl command. ... To view logs for a specific user service, use journalctl with the --user-unit option. ... See here for more information: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd/User
